name: Nora Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is a normal shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and a junior operator loading glass and film into a solar-panel laminator on nights. I finished secondary school and still ask the lead to check my first temperature setting. The clean pane is satisfying; finding trapped air after a full rack has run is the rough part.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are pay, family and AI use for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner manages a restaurant. We have two school-age children and a mortgage, with about ten months of expenses saved. The night premium gives me higher factory pay, and plenty of similar plants are nearby. I use AI every day for fault notes, but check it against the machine log and actual glass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our laminate crew AI is handy for sorting the process log, but somebody still has to spot a trapped bubble in a solar panel before the glass goes into the press. That's a real eye check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I earn a high night rate although I'm junior on this line. My partner manages a restaurant and we have ten months of household expenses saved, a mortgage and two school-age children. Plenty of nearby factories hire, so this mild change leaves us secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep loading glass and film into the solar-panel laminator, checking the first pane with the lead. I already use AI every day to draft fault notes, then compare them with the machine log. I'll keep adding new money from full wages to our reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little curiosity about a better log. I can improve this machine skill without changing jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the AI summary miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week the AI summary called a bubble a harmless mark. I held the first pane under the inspection lamp and the lead confirmed trapped air before we ran the next rack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do your rosters fit at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner's restaurant is busiest when I am home after a night shift, so we compare the rota on Sundays. We do not spend the emergency reserve on a new tool just because it has a polished screen.

say: **AI process logs** can improve while trapped air still needs a physical glass check.
The **first solar pane** must pass an inspection lamp before a full rack runs.
think: My **high night wage** and restaurant income continue here.
Ten months of **savings** and many nearby factories give us a strong buffer.
do: **Keep** loading solar glass and checking the first laminated pane under the inspection lamp.
**Add** new savings from full night-rate wages.
feel: **Calm** about secure pay and modest log improvements.
S0.quote: I held the first pane under the inspection lamp and the lead confirmed trapped air before we ran the next rack.
fieldNote: Nora uses **AI daily** but verifies fault summaries against glass and machine records.
Her **strong ten-month reserve** supports calm while two household wages and local factory options remain reliable.

steps.text: Keep loading solar-panel laminator and inspecting first panes
Add new savings from full night-rate wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the shift AI may improve orders and inspection reports before a robot can move a hot pane safely. I'd like operators included when the factory decides which defects a new camera can reject.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own night wage looks safe for now because the physical layup still needs hands. The restaurant may use faster booking software, but my partner still has diners to serve and staff to manage. I want to test tools early if I can compare them with real panels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask for a paid supervised place on the new AI defect-classification screen and learn how to correct its labels on five rejected panes if offered. I'll record which marks are actual bubbles, then show the quality lead before any automatic rejection is switched on. I'll keep my current line shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a camera making a bad rejection at scale, not expecting a cut to our income yet. I want to be in the test before a pallet is scrapped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which panes would test the new screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The five panes should include a trapped bubble, a surface smear and a clean edge. I would check each under the lamp, then correct the AI label rather than just read its verdict.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you use the classification result?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the quality lead finds the screen consistent, we can trial it on one isolated rack. I am asking for the paid session; the factory has not offered the place yet.

say: **AI inspection** may speed reports while operators still need to inspect actual panes.
A **quality lead** should review corrected labels before automatic rejection.
think: Our **household pay** looks intact in this slower picture.
A mistaken **camera label** could scrap good panels or miss trapped air.
do: **Learn** AI label corrections if a real paid place is offered.
**Keep** current laminate shifts while checking five panels.
feel: **Uneasy** about faulty classification with secure current pay.
S1.quote: I want to be in the test before a pallet is scrapped.
fieldNote: Her **new AI skill** is correcting defect labels, beyond existing daily note drafting.
The paid screen session is **requested**, with learning conditional on an actual offered place.

steps.text: Learn AI defect-label correction if paid supervised place offered
Keep laminate shifts and inspect five test panes with lead

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI by 2028 could plan the panel runs, then capable robots around 2031 could lay up, move and inspect the glass. I'd tell the crew we should test the robot stop and find paid roles before anyone shortens the line roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when capable robots reach our physical work. Ten months saved and plenty of local plants give choices, but losing my high night rate would change the mortgage budget. I like technology, yet I don't assume a robot creates as many operator jobs as it removes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask the engineering lead for a paid supervised robot-cell trial and a funded recognized safety-controls course with an actual place. If offered, I'll attend and practise stopping a pane lift on an isolated rack. After qualifying, if my line hours fall, I'll apply for posted local robot-setter jobs only if the safe duties, regular hours and base pay cover our household costs; if no course appears, I'll apply for posted local production jobs at adequate pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the wage even with savings. I can move fast, but I want a real paid place and a real vacancy before putting the mortgage on a new title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safe robot test include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The practical test should include a pane that starts to slip, an accessible stop and a worker outside the lift zone. A robot sales film cannot prove that the glass won't fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you assess a setter vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the setter posting's base wage with our mortgage, food and school transport, then check whether its shifts fit our children's care. Overtime on a brochure would not settle it.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes planning before robots handle glass around 2031.
Operators need **paid safety practice** and actual future roles.
think: At **48**, lost night pay could disrupt the mortgage budget.
Ten months of **savings** and local factories offer time, not guaranteed equal wages.
do: **Request** a paid robot-cell trial and funded place.
**Attend** supervised safety-controls training if offered with paid time.
**Apply** to posted qualified local setter work if hours fall and pay suffices.
feel: **Anxious** about possible loss of higher paid shifts.
S2.quote: A robot sales film cannot prove that the glass won't fall.
fieldNote: She distinguishes a **trial request** from offered paid supervised practice and a recognized course.
The **qualified setter application** and no-course production fallback require real local postings and sufficient pay.

steps.text: Ask engineering lead for paid supervised robot-cell trial
Attend funded safety-controls course if paid isolated place offered
Apply for posted safe local setter job if qualified, cuts, base pay and care hours fit
Apply to posted local production job if no course appears and pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If thinking AI changes panel plans by 2031 and capable robots handle glass around 2034, I'd tell the shift five years is enough to run proper tests. A paid role has to be posted before anyone calls training a future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 51 when robots reach the laminator. The children will be older, but we may still need the higher night rate and the mortgage may still run. I can gain a second machine skill without leaving paid work if the factory offers a real place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the laminate shift and save new money from every full premium month. If the plant offers a recognized robot-setter certificate with funded fees, paid release and isolated supervised lifts, I'll enrol next year. After qualifying, if night hours are cut, I'll apply to posted local setter roles only if safe duties, regular pay and shifts meet our household needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible loss of the higher rate, though I have time to test a route. I would rather learn the stop control on a real machine than collect a certificate from a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a practical assessment test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to mark a trapped bubble before the lift, then stop a slipping pane on the guarded rack. The instructor should check my response before I work near a live line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should a local posting show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A factory posting should say who can stop the robot and what the base rate is. If it only promises future opportunities, I'll keep earning on the present line.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes planning before robots handle panels around 2034.
A **posted paid role** must follow useful guarded training.
think: At **51**, I may still need the higher night rate for our mortgage.
A **real course place** lets me learn while earning.
do: **Keep** the laminate wage and add new savings.
**Enrol** in recognized setter course if fees, paid release and safe lifts covered.
**Apply** to posted safe local setters after qualifying if hours fall and pay fits.
feel: **Anxious** about later rate loss with time for paid practice.
S3.quote: I would rather learn the stop control on a real machine than collect a certificate from a screen.
fieldNote: New **savings** come from future full premium months, not the existing reserve.
The **application** is separate from enrolment and retains qualification, reduced hours, safe duties and enough posted pay.

steps.text: Save new money from full paid laminate premium months
Enrol in recognized setter course if funded paid guarded place offered
Apply for posted safe local setter role if qualified, hours cut, pay sufficient

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2036 might plan panels, and capable robots around 2039 might lift and inspect glass. I'd tell the crew a decade gives us time to practise stop controls before any new line is trusted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 56 when robots handle the physical line. Our children may be grown, but we still expect to work and possibly pay the mortgage. Ten months saved now and a high wage give us room to build skills over ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the paid night shift and add new savings from each full premium month. I'll learn the plant's new AI defect-correction controls on a paid supervised test rack if it offers one, then take a recognized robot-setter course only if the plant funds fees and paid guarded practice. If robots later cut hours, I'll apply after qualifying only to posted safe local roles with sufficient regular pay and workable shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later job numbers, but curious about what we can learn over a decade. Our present wages look secure while the panel work is still paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you learn new defect controls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare ten AI defect labels with actual lamp inspections and correct each wrong label. If the screen becomes dependable, it could save rework before a robot ever lifts the glass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you leave the night shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a real posting with base pay and a shift that fits family responsibilities. A course alone is not income; I would keep the night wage until a suitable offer exists.

say: **2036 thinking AI** changes planning before robots lift panels around 2039.
A **decade** allows checked AI labels and guarded stop-control practice.
think: At **56**, I may still need work and mortgage income.
The **strong reserve** and high wage support a gradual route, not guaranteed future work.
do: **Keep** paid night work and add new savings.
**Learn** defect-correction controls if paid supervised rack offered.
**Enrol** in funded guarded setter training, then apply after cuts if qualified to posted safe local work at sufficient pay.
feel: **Uneasy** about later roles with secure present wages.
S4.quote: A course alone is not income; I would keep the night wage until a suitable offer exists.
fieldNote: Her **adaptive approach** includes genuinely new AI control learning and guarded practical qualification.
Any later **job application** depends on posted safe local work, qualification, cut hours and adequate pay.

steps.text: Save new money from full paid night-premium months
Learn AI defect controls if paid supervised test rack offered
Enrol in setter course if funded paid guarded place offered

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could lift and inspect panels while my higher night wage pays the mortgage. A real paid safety-controls place and posted local setter work at enough base pay would give me a route.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who catches a bubble trapped in the first solar pane after a robot stacks the rack. A clean production total cannot make trapped air disappear from a panel.

headlineQuote: A clean production total cannot make trapped air disappear from a panel.
portrait: **Nora**, 43, is a junior solar-panel laminator operator with secondary school education and a high night rate.
She and her restaurant-manager partner support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage with ten months saved.
She uses **AI daily**, checking outputs against logs and real glass, and seeks new safe controls early.
Fast robots make her **anxious** about paid shifts, while the long runway supports conditional training and local applications.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable panel-handling robots around 2031 and cut her higher paid night shifts.
whatWouldHelp: An offered **paid safety-controls place** and posted safe local setter role at enough base pay would help.
